title: DKA and HHS
blurb: Confirm DKA with D, K and A, run the fixed-rate insulin infusion, fluids and potassium safely, and tell DKA apart from the slower, more dangerous-to-rush HHS.
question: Ms Kowal, 19, with type 1 diabetes, has a glucose of 24 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.2 mmol/L and venous pH 7.18. A fixed-rate insulin infusion is being prescribed. What should happen to her usual long-acting insulin?

teach.body: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) happens when there is too little insulin: the body burns fat, ketones build up and the blood becomes acidic. It develops over hours, typically in type 1 diabetes. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) develops over days, usually in older people with type 2 diabetes: glucose climbs very high and the person becomes severely dehydrated, but without significant ketones or acidosis. Plain English: DKA is an acid problem; HHS is a water problem.

letters.word: Diabetes: glucose above 11.0 mmol/L or known diabetes
Ketones: blood above 3.0 mmol/L or urine 2+
Acidosis: bicarbonate below 15.0 and/or venous pH below 7.3

teach.caption: Mixed DKA and HHS is common; treat significant ketonaemia with acidosis on the DKA pathway.

steps.label: Fluids
steps.sub: 0.9% sodium chloride; 1 L over the first hour if SBP 90+

steps.label: Potassium
steps.sub: Added to each litre after the first, by level

teach.caption: If systolic BP is below 90 mmHg, give 500 mL over 10–15 minutes and seek senior input.

teach.h: Potassium in each litre of fluid
head: Potassium (mmol/L)
Add per litre
teach.caption: Insulin drives potassium into cells, so levels fall as treatment works. Call the doctor if potassium is not kept between 4.0 and 5.5 mmol/L.

teach.body: Check capillary glucose and ketones hourly, and venous gas (pH, bicarbonate, potassium) at 60 minutes, 2 hours, then 2-hourly. Targets: ketones fall at least 0.5 mmol/L/h, bicarbonate rises 3 mmol/L/h, glucose falls 3 mmol/L/h. If not, check the pump and line, then ask for a rate increase. DKA has resolved when ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH is above 7.3. Stop the FRIII 30 minutes after subcutaneous short-acting insulin.
teach.cite: JBDS 02 pathway; JBDS nursing guide v1.0 (Dec 2022)

teach.text: Do not judge DKA by glucose. Glucose falls long before the acid clears, and SGLT-2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose. When glucose drops below 14, keep the insulin going and add 10% glucose. Resolution is ketones below 0.6 and pH above 7.3, not a normal glucose or bicarbonate alone.

teach.body: Mr Douglas, a care home resident with type 2 diabetes, has had a chest infection for 4 days. He is drowsy and very dry. Glucose 46, ketones 0.8, pH 7.36, calculated osmolality 352. The nurse expects 0.9% sodium chloride first, osmolality hourly for 6 hours, and insulin held until glucose stops falling with fluids. She keeps a strict fluid balance chart, protects his heels and checks his feet daily, and gives the prescribed prophylactic LMWH.

items.label: mmol in 24 h: maximum change in sodium

teach.caption: Calculated osmolality = 2 x Na + glucose + urea. Rapid shifts risk cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination.

items: DKA = glucose above 11 (or known diabetes) + ketones above 3.0 + bicarbonate below 15 and/or pH below 7.3.
FRIII 0.1 units/kg/h; keep usual basal insulin; 10% glucose at 125 mL/h once glucose is below 14.
Potassium per litre: none above 5.5, 40 mmol at 3.5–5.5, senior review below 3.5.
Resolved: ketones below 0.6 and venous pH above 7.3.
HHS: glucose 30+, osmolality 320+, fluids first, slow correction, heels protected, LMWH.

summary: You can now confirm DKA against all three criteria, support FRIII, fluids and potassium safely, and monitor towards true resolution. You can also recognise HHS and explain why it is corrected slowly with fluids first.

A.q: Ms Kowal, 19, has type 1 diabetes, glucose 24 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.2 mmol/L and venous pH 7.18. A fixed-rate IV insulin infusion is started. What should happen to her usual long-acting insulin?
options: Stop it while the infusion runs
Give it once DKA has resolved
A.why: JBDS 02: continue the person's usual long-acting basal insulin alongside the FRIII. It prevents rebound ketosis when the infusion stops.

whyNot.0: Stopping basal insulin risks rebound DKA when the infusion is stopped.
whyNot.1: JBDS continues the usual basal dose; it does not halve it in DKA.
whyNot.3: Waiting until resolution leaves a gap in background insulin.

A.q: Which set of results confirms diabetic ketoacidosis?
A.why: JBDS 02: DKA needs glucose above 11.0 (or known diabetes), blood ketones above 3.0 mmol/L, and bicarbonate below 15 and/or venous pH below 7.3. Only this set meets all three.

whyNot.0: Ketones 1.2 and pH 7.35 do not meet the K or A criteria.
whyNot.1: Very high glucose without ketones or acidosis suggests HHS, not DKA.
whyNot.2: Ketones 2.1 and pH 7.31 fall short of the K and A thresholds.

A.q: Mr Ahmed weighs 80 kg and is in DKA. What is the initial fixed-rate insulin infusion rate?
A.why: JBDS 02: FRIII at 0.1 units/kg/h. 80 kg x 0.1 = 8 units per hour.

whyNot.1: 4 units/h is 0.05 units/kg/h, the reduced rate considered once glucose is below 14.
whyNot.2: 6 units/h would be correct for 60 kg, not 80 kg.

B.q: Before the second litre of fluid in DKA, Mr Ahmed's potassium is 4.6 mmol/L. How much potassium chloride should be in that litre?
B.why: JBDS 02: potassium 3.5–5.5 mmol/L, add 40 mmol potassium chloride per litre.

whyNot.0: No potassium is added when it is above 5.5 mmol/L.
whyNot.1: 20 mmol is not the JBDS replacement for this band.
whyNot.3: Higher amounts need senior review when potassium is below 3.5.

B.q: Four hours into DKA treatment, Ms Kowal's glucose is 12.8 mmol/L but ketones are 2.4 mmol/L. What should happen next?
options: Stop the FRIII as glucose is near normal
B.why: JBDS 02: when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, add 10% glucose at 125 mL/h and continue insulin (consider reducing to 0.05 units/kg/h) until ketones are below 0.6 and pH above 7.3.

whyNot.0: Ketones are still high; stopping insulin lets the acidosis return.
whyNot.2: Conversion happens after resolution and when she is eating, not while ketones are 2.4.
whyNot.3: She is not hypoglycaemic; a glucose infusion alongside insulin is needed instead.

B.q: During DKA treatment, ketones have fallen by only 0.2 mmol/L in the past hour. What should the nurse check first?
options: That the infusion pump and line are working
That the patient has eaten breakfast
That the 10% glucose is running faster
That the basal insulin has been omitted
B.why: JBDS nursing guide: if ketones are not falling by at least 0.5 mmol/L/h, check the pump is working and connected with the correct residual volume, then call the prescriber to increase the rate by 1 unit/h.

whyNot.1: Eating does not explain failure to clear ketones on a FRIII.
whyNot.2: Faster glucose is not the response to slowly falling ketones.
whyNot.3: Basal insulin should be continued, not omitted.

C.q: Mr Douglas, 78, has type 2 diabetes and a 4-day chest infection. Glucose 46 mmol/L, ketones 0.8, pH 7.36, osmolality 352 mOsm/kg. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Oral fluids and his usual gliclazide
C.why: JBDS 06: HHS is treated with IV 0.9% sodium chloride first; insulin (0.05 units/kg/h) is started when glucose stops falling with fluids, unless there is significant ketonaemia.

whyNot.0: FRIII at DKA rates is for DKA or mixed DKA/HHS; his ketones and pH are not in that range.
whyNot.1: 0.45% saline is used if osmolality is not falling despite adequate positive balance, not first.
whyNot.3: He is drowsy and severely dehydrated; oral treatment is unsafe and inadequate.

C.q: In HHS treatment, Mr Douglas's glucose falls from 46 to 34 mmol/L in the first hour. What is the concern?
options: Too slow: insulin should be doubled
C.why: JBDS 06: glucose should fall by no more than 5 mmol/L/h and osmolality by 3–8 mOsm/kg/h. A 12 mmol/L fall risks cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination.

whyNot.0: The fall is already too rapid; more insulin would worsen it.
whyNot.2: A fall of 12 mmol/L in an hour exceeds the safe rate.
whyNot.3: Hypotonic fluid would speed osmotic shifts further.

C.q: Ms Kowal's ketones are now 0.4 mmol/L, venous pH 7.36, and she is eating. Her rapid-acting insulin is given at 08:00 with breakfast. When should the FRIII be stopped?
C.why: JBDS 02: DKA has resolved (ketones below 0.6, pH above 7.3). Do not discontinue the IV insulin infusion until 30 minutes after subcutaneous short-acting insulin has been given.

whyNot.0: Stopping before the injection leaves a gap with no active insulin.
whyNot.1: Subcutaneous insulin takes time to act; an overlap of 30 minutes is needed.
whyNot.2: Running the infusion for 4 hours after the injection risks hypoglycaemia.

reteach.title: Acid versus water
reteach.question: If DKA is an acid problem and HHS is a water problem, what does each one need first?

blocks.body: DKA (acid): give fluid and switch on the insulin straight away at 0.1 units/kg/h, keep basal insulin, replace potassium, add glucose when below 14, and do not stop until ketones are below 0.6 and pH above 7.3. HHS (water): give 0.9% sodium chloride first and let fluid alone bring glucose down, slowly. Add low-dose insulin (0.05 units/kg/h) when glucose stops falling.

blocks.text: Normal glucose does not mean DKA is over. Check ketones and pH.

explain.body: D: glucose above 11.0 or known diabetes. K: ketones above 3.0 or urine 2+. A: bicarbonate below 15.0 and/or venous pH below 7.3. All three are needed before an FRIII.

test.q: A man taking an SGLT-2 inhibitor has glucose 10.2 mmol/L, ketones 4.6 mmol/L, pH 7.19. He has known type 2 diabetes. Does he meet the DKA criteria?
options: Yes: known diabetes meets the D criterion
test.why: JBDS 02: the D criterion is glucose above 11.0 OR known diabetes. With ketones above 3.0 and pH below 7.3, this is DKA (euglycaemic DKA is a recognised SGLT-2 inhibitor risk).

whyNot.1: Known diabetes satisfies D even with glucose below 11.
whyNot.2: DKA occurs in type 2 diabetes, including with SGLT-2 inhibitors.
whyNot.3: pH below 7.0 is a severity marker, not the diagnostic threshold.

explain.body: FRIII 0.1 units/kg/h (50 units soluble insulin in 50 mL 0.9% sodium chloride). Continue basal insulin. When glucose is below 14, add 10% glucose at 125 mL/h and consider 0.05 units/kg/h.

test.q: At what rate does JBDS run 10% glucose once glucose falls below 14 mmol/L in DKA?
test.why: JBDS 02: add 10% glucose at 125 mL/h alongside the sodium chloride when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L.

whyNot.0: 75 mL/h is not the JBDS rate.
whyNot.2: 250 mL/h is double the JBDS rate.
whyNot.3: 500 mL/h is far higher than the JBDS rate.

explain.body: 1 L 0.9% sodium chloride over the first hour (if SBP 90+), then further litres with potassium over 2, 2, 4, 4 and 6 hours. Potassium: none above 5.5, 40 mmol per litre at 3.5–5.5, senior review below 3.5.

test.q: A woman in DKA has a potassium of 5.9 mmol/L before her second litre. What should be added?
test.why: JBDS 02: if potassium is above 5.5 mmol/L, add no potassium; recheck on the next venous gas.

whyNot.1: 20 mmol is not a JBDS band, and any added potassium is inappropriate above 5.5.
whyNot.3: 10 mmol still adds potassium when the level is already above 5.5; JBDS adds none.

explain.body: Glucose 30+, osmolality usually 320+, ketones 3.0 or below, pH 7.3+. Fluids first. Osmolality hourly for 6 hours, falling 3–8 mOsm/kg/h; glucose no faster than 5 mmol/L/h. Heels protected, daily foot checks, LMWH for most.

test.q: Which nursing measure does JBDS specifically highlight for people with HHS?
options: Fluid restriction to 1.5 L a day
Heel protection and daily foot checks
Bed rest with legs elevated on pillows
test.why: JBDS 06: everyone with HHS should be assumed to be at high risk of foot ulceration; protect heels and check feet daily.

whyNot.0: People with HHS are severely dehydrated and need fluid replacement.
whyNot.2: Blood cultures are taken if infection is suspected, not hourly.
whyNot.3: Bed rest with leg elevation is not a JBDS HHS measure; JBDS asks for heels to be off-loaded and feet checked daily, with LMWH for VTE risk.
